messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Prison Guard
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 35

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts, Drop Responsibilities: give up important responsibilities to stay safe or avoid triggers, Checking Surroundings: constantly scan environment for signs of threat
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
  Negative Appraisals: Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Vignette:
Nadia Haddad is a 68-year-old married prison guard who came to treatment after months of telling herself she was managing well enough. The assault happened on an evening shift in a housing unit that had gone unusually quiet just before count. She still remembers that silence with particular clarity: the kind of silence that felt wrong in a prison, when the usual metal clatter, voices, and movement suddenly dropped away. Nadia had been standing with another officer near the tier when an inmate rushed them. The attack was fast and close. What has stayed with her most is not only her own fear, but the instant she realized the other officer was exposed and she could not stop what was happening. Even now, when she speaks about it, her thoughts return to that moment with harsh certainty: she should have protected the other person, should have seen it coming, should have done more. The fact that she survived and returned to work has not softened that belief.

In the weeks afterward, Nadia did not describe herself as shaken so much as altered. She had spent decades in correctional work and had prided herself on reading a unit, reading people, knowing when trouble was building. After the assault, she no longer trusted that sense. She had come to believe that people could turn without warning and that trust itself was dangerous. At work she began scanning constantly—doorways, hands, corners of rooms, changes in tone, any break in the usual rhythm of the block. If a range became too quiet, her body reacted before she had fully registered why: her shoulders tightened, her breath shortened, and she felt a jolt of alarm as if another attack were already underway. She found it hard to explain this to her husband except to say that her body “knows before my mind does.” Silence frightened her more than shouting. Noise at least meant she could locate where people were. Silence, to her, suggested planning, concealment, danger gathering out of sight.

Sleep became difficult in a way that felt both exhausting and humiliating. Nadia would lie awake listening for sounds inside and outside the house, unable to settle if the rooms seemed too still. On some nights she drifted off only to wake again quickly, alert and tense, as though called back to duty by something she could not name. She began dreading the nighttime quiet in her own home. Her husband noticed she left the television on later than before or called family members in the evening for no real reason. Nadia knew she was doing it partly to avoid being alone with her thoughts. If cousins dropped by, or if she stayed on the phone, or if she arranged coffee with neighbors, there was less room for the memory of that silent unit and the conviction that she had failed someone who depended on her.

Over time, being around people became one of the main ways she got through the day. She kept herself surrounded whenever she could, lingering after shifts, agreeing to gatherings she would once have skipped, filling empty hours so that she did not have to sit quietly. Yet this did not bring ease. She often felt apart even in company, as though the assault had put her on the outside of ordinary life. Among coworkers she felt older, more exposed, less sure of where she stood. Around family she could smile and talk, but privately she believed they did not fully understand what had changed in her. She had come to feel that she was permanently an outsider now, someone who could not rejoin the uncomplicated trust other people seemed to have.

Her work life narrowed as well. Nadia began dropping responsibilities she had previously handled without hesitation. She asked not to take on certain posts, backed away from tasks that would leave her in situations that felt too exposed, and let others cover duties she once considered part of her role. She framed these decisions as practical, as staying safe, but they carried consequences. Coworkers noticed. Some were sympathetic; others seemed impatient. Nadia felt ashamed each time she stepped back, and that shame fed the same thought: when it mattered, she had failed to protect someone, and now she could not be counted on in the same way.

What finally brought her to seek help was not a single crisis but the accumulation of these changes. After another night of little sleep, she froze during a silent stretch on the unit and felt her body surge into alarm before anything had happened. Later at home, sitting with her husband in a room that had gone briefly still, she realized she no longer felt safe even in ordinary quiet. She is seeking help now because she does not want the rest of her life organized around vigilance, sleeplessness, and staying surrounded by people. At the same time, what frightens her most is the possibility that her fear is justified—that silence really does mean danger, that people truly cannot be trusted, and that the part of her that once believed otherwise is gone for good.
